Modern.tagline: Where the kitchen meets the table.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Pass is the kitchen word for the surface where the chef plates and calls the dish before it goes to the room. Cooks stand on the line. The chef stands at the pass. The brand sits at the moment the kitchen lets go.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern restaurants are competing on more than the food. The menu, the room, the booking flow, the social presence all carry weight. Brand is doing work it didn't do ten years ago. The clean modern restaurants stand out by saying less.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Misi (misinewyork.com) showed how restraint reads as confidence. King (kingrestaurant.nyc) earns trust by being clear about everything. Atomix (atomixnyc.com) carries a strong design language across plate and menu. We borrow the discipline from these and the openness of a neighborhood place.
Modern.positioningStatement: Modern dining for people who pick the restaurant before they pick the menu.

targetAudience.primary: 28 to 45. Lives in a city. Eats out twice a week. Reads the menu before they arrive. Tips well. Books for two but invites a third when the room is right.

dos: Show the price next to it
donts: Describe a dish as a journey

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. PASS in a tight grotesk, all caps, set with a single thin horizontal rule beneath it. The rule is the pass surface. The mark works on a menu, a window, and a takeaway box.

colorPalette.name: Service Black
colorPalette.meaning: Apron color. The dark of a closed kitchen at midnight.

colorPalette.name: Citrus
colorPalette.meaning: Lemon zest. The single bright accent in a quiet plate.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and menu headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for prices and dish numbers
typography.rationale: One family. The regular weight names the food. The mono carries the facts. The customer reads both clearly.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No tasting menu prose. No farm-to-table copy. No chalkboard daily specials in cursive. No emoji on the menu.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A single printed menu, reprinted weekly. A two-line confirmation email. A web page that loads in under a second. A line out the door, kept moving.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: The Long Table is a piece of furniture, an idea, and a tradition. A single table where the meal lasts as long as the conversation. The definite article makes it singular. The name sets the expectation before the first course.
Luxury.story: We built The Long Table because we missed the kind of dinner that ran long. The kind that ends with the kitchen lights off and the staff sitting down to eat with you. So we built a room with one table that seats fourteen, and a kitchen that cooks for that table only.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end dining has gotten faster, more turn-driven, more producer-led. There's a thin market at the other end. Slow rooms. One seating. People who book three months out for an evening that runs four hours.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Frenchette (frenchettenewyork.com) carries the classical New York room. Le Bernardin (le-bernardin.com) is the institution we admire from a distance. Estela (estelanyc.com) has the warmth. None of them are this small.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A restaurant for one table of fourteen, one seating, four nights a week.

targetAudience.primary: 40 to 70. Has eaten everywhere. Looking for somewhere new only if it's not actually new. Pays for the room and the time, not the prestige.

dos: Address the guest by name in writing
Send the menu the day before, in print

Luxury.logoDirection: A wordmark in a classical serif with thin caps and elegant ligatures. A small horizontal line beneath the words, the long table itself, reduced. Used on the front door, on the printed menu, and in a single embossed corner of every linen napkin.

colorPalette.name: Wine Dark
colorPalette.meaning: The color of the third glass.

colorPalette.name: Brass
colorPalette.meaning: Cutlery, candleholders, the small lamp on the table.

colorPalette.name: Olive Black
colorPalette.meaning: Aged wood, cured leather, the menu cover.

typography.primary: Canela for the wordmark and printed menu
typography.secondary: Söhne for guest correspondence and reservation pages
typography.rationale: A high contrast serif carries the room. A modern grotesk handles the few digital surfaces. Nothing decorative.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No à la carte. No private buyouts. No social media presence. No second location. No press.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Names the place on the table where shared dishes sit. The brand puts the middle of the table in the brand position. Plain. Specific. Honest about the format.
Minimal.industrySummary: Sharing plates is the way most people prefer to eat in cities. The format has become standard. The category has not had a brand that puts the idea front and center.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Brutalisten (brutalisten.com) takes the philosophy further than we will. Sqirl (sqirlla.com) built a different cult around the same idea. Most sharing-plate places hide the concept under generic names. We don't.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A neighborhood restaurant where every dish is meant for the middle of the table.

targetAudience.primary: Couples, friend groups, people who eat out as a way to spend time, not just to eat. They order too much and they take the leftovers home.

dos: Name the dish, name the price
Recommend three plates for two people
donts: Photograph plates from above with a single sprig of dill

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. MIDDLE in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps. No icon. The wordmark on the door, the menu, and the takeaway box. The D's vertical stroke aligns with the I to suggest the center of a table.

colorPalette.name: Olive
colorPalette.meaning: Single warm accent. The color of one good ingredient.

typography.rationale: One face. One job. Nothing decorative.

customSections.title: Not this
customSections.body: No tasting menu. No reservations longer than two hours. No private dining. No music after the second course.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Boardman sounds like a person who has been doing this since the 1950s. The & Co. closes it like a real, established firm. The name reads as something a Fortune 500 already has under contract.
Corporate.industrySummary: Corporate dining is a category most people don't think about until they're the buyer. Companies want clean food, predictable service, and a vendor who can handle multiple offices on one contract. The market is mostly served by older institutional caterers and a few new white-label players.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Compass Group (compass-group.com) is the giant. Restaurant Associates (restaurantassociatesinc.com) is the premium-leaning operator. Bon Appetit Management (bamco.com) sits in the middle. We are smaller, more design-led, and more flexible than any of them.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Corporate dining services for companies that consider the lunch hour part of the workplace.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Most buyers haven't thought about their cafeteria provider in five years. We win by showing up better than the incumbent on day one, with data, with consistency, and with food employees actually like.

targetAudience.primary: Heads of facilities, real estate, and people operations at companies of 500 to 25000 employees. They sign the contract and they catch the complaints.

dos: Speak to the buyer, not the diner
donts: Photograph the food on a kitchen counter

messagingPillars.name: One vendor across sites
messagingPillars.description: We run the cafeteria, the catering, the conference dining, and the reporting under one contract.

messagingPillars.name: Real participation
messagingPillars.description: We measure who actually eats with us, not who signed up. The number that matters is the daily count.

messagingPillars.name: Procurement-ready reporting
messagingPillars.description: Monthly utilization, allergen reports, ESG-aligned sourcing data. Formatted the way procurement uses it.

Corporate.logoDirection: A wordmark with a small geometric mark to the left. The mark is a single olive branch reduced to two strokes, suggesting nourishment without being literal. Reads cleanly on uniforms, vans, and procurement decks.

colorPalette.name: Olive
colorPalette.meaning: A quiet accent. The color of a good ingredient.

typography.secondary: Source Serif Pro for printed quarterly reports
typography.rationale: Inter scales clean across digital and operational signage. Serif reserved for printed B2B documents.

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No retail restaurants. No D2C meal kits. No celebrity chef partnerships. No flashy openings.

Creative.tagline: Stay hungry. We'll handle the rest.
Creative.brandNameRationale: One word. Loud. It names the thing the customer brings in and the thing the restaurant returns. The word works on a sign, a totebag, a neon, a menu cover. Says everything before you read the menu.
Creative.manifesto: We started Appetite because most restaurants are too quiet about being restaurants. They whisper their names. They hide their menus. They photograph their dishes like museum pieces. We wanted a place that's loud about being fun and quiet about being good, instead of the other way around.
Creative.industrySummary: Modern restaurants got serious. Concept-driven, minimal, quiet. There's room for one that's loud, warm, full of personality, and still puts out food that holds up under criticism.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Carbone (mainecarbone.com) figured out maximalist done right. Bavette (bavettesteakhouse.com) sells the room as much as the steak. Major Food Group's restaurants have the playbook. We're smaller and weirder.
Creative.positioningStatement: A restaurant with the personality of a bar and the food of a kitchen that means it.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 40. Eats out four nights a week. Brings friends. Drinks more than they should. Posts the menu cover, not the plate. Buys the merch.

dos: Talk like the host who's already had a drink

Creative.logoDirection: A wordmark in a punchy serif with the second P stylized as a fork tine. A standalone fork-tine icon for stickers, totebags, and Instagram profile pictures. The mark looks great in neon on a wall.

colorPalette.name: Appetite Red
colorPalette.meaning: Hunger. Heat. The check at the end of the night.

colorPalette.name: Butter
colorPalette.meaning: Pure warmth. The pat on the bread plate.

colorPalette.name: Wine Dark
colorPalette.meaning: Anchoring deep red. The third glass.

typography.primary: Migra for the wordmark and big display
typography.secondary: PP Neue Montreal for body and signage
typography.rationale: Migra carries the personality. Neue Montreal handles the menu and the website. The pair feels expensive and a little weird.

customSections.title: What it isn't
customSections.body: Not minimal. Not concept driven. Not a chef brand. Not photographed in natural light.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: Totebags people actually wear. Stickers on phone cases. A printed menu that the host hands you, never on a tablet. Neon on the wall. A merch wall in the bathroom hallway.
